questions.stem: When a fast-moving bus suddenly stops, passengers are thrown forward. This is a classic demonstration of:

options.option_text: Newton's First Law of Motion (Law of Inertia)
Newton's Second Law of Motion
Newton's Third Law of Motion
The Law of Conservation of Momentum

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia) states that an object in motion stays in motion with the same speed and in the same direction unless acted upon by an unbalanced force. When the bus stops, the lower part of the passenger's body (in contact with the seat) stops with the bus, but the upper part of the body continues moving forward due to inertia of motion.
DECOY BUSTING: The Second Law (F=ma) relates force, mass, and acceleration. The Third Law (Action/Reaction) explains rocket propulsion. Conservation of momentum applies to collisions.
EXAM INSIGHT: Galileo was the first to formulate the concept of inertia. Newton simply built upon it. Another common example: dusting a carpet by beating it with a stick (dust particles remain at rest due to inertia of rest while the carpet moves away).

questions.stem: According to Newton's Second Law of Motion, the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to:

options.option_text: The applied unbalanced force
The mass of the body
The velocity of the body
The inertia of the body

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Newton's Second Law states that the rate of change of momentum of an object is directly proportional to the unbalanced force applied on it, and the change takes place in the direction of the force. Since momentum (p) = mass (m) x velocity (v), and assuming mass is constant, the rate of change of velocity is acceleration (a). Thus, we get the famous equation: Force (F) = mass (m) x acceleration (a).
DECOY BUSTING: While force depends on mass and velocity (momentum), the LAW itself states it is proportional to the APPLIED FORCE. 
EXAM INSIGHT: A fielder in cricket pulls his hands backward while catching a fast ball to increase the TIME taken to stop the ball. By increasing time, the rate of change of momentum decreases, meaning a smaller force is applied to his hands (preventing injury).

questions.stem: A rocket works on the principle of conservation of momentum. Which of Newton's laws is the fundamental driving force behind rocket propulsion?

options.option_text: Newton's Third Law of Motion
Newton's First Law of Motion
Newton's Second Law of Motion
Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Newton's Third Law states that "for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction." A rocket engine forcefully expels high-speed, burning exhaust gases backward (the Action). In response, the exhaust gases push the rocket forward with an equal amount of force (the Reaction).
DECOY BUSTING: The First Law is about inertia. The Second Law determines how fast the rocket will accelerate given its mass and thrust. But the actual mechanism of getting pushed forward in a vacuum (where there is no air to push against) relies entirely on the Third Law.
EXAM INSIGHT: Other classic examples of the Third Law include the recoil of a gun when a bullet is fired, swimming (pushing water backward to move forward), and walking (pushing the ground backward).

questions.stem: A spinning top continues to rotate about its own axis even after the external spin is applied and removed. This behaviour is best classified as which type of inertia?

options.option_text: Inertia of rest, resisting any change in a stationary body
Inertia of direction, resisting any change in the rotation axis
Inertia of motion, resisting any change in a body's state of motion
Inertia of mass, which depends solely on gravitational attraction

questions.explanation: C is correct because the top is already in rotational motion and continues due to inertia of motion — resistance to any change in an existing state of motion. Option B is wrong: inertia of direction applies to a body moving in a straight path that resists turning, not to a spinning body maintaining its rotational state.

questions.stem: A horse pulls a cart forward by exerting a force on it. According to Newton's Third Law, which statement correctly identifies the reaction force to this pull?

options.option_text: Ground pushes the horse forward with an equal and opposite force
Cart pulls the horse backward with a force equal in magnitude
Friction on the cart wheels provides an equal forward reaction force
Weight of the cart acts downward as a reaction to the horse's pull

questions.explanation: B is correct: the action-reaction pair under Newton's Third Law must act on different bodies — the horse pulls the cart forward, so the cart pulls the horse backward with equal magnitude. Option A describes a different action-reaction pair (ground-horse friction pair), not the direct reaction to the horse's pull on the cart.

questions.stem: A fielder in cricket gradually lowers and draws back his hands while catching a fast ball, rather than keeping his hands rigid at the point of impact. The primary physical principle behind this technique is that it?

options.option_text: Increases the total impulse received from the ball by the fielder
Increases the time of impact, thereby reducing the average force on the hands
Decreases the total change in momentum of the ball during the catch
Reduces the ball's velocity before contact with the fielder's palms

questions.explanation: B is correct: by the impulse-momentum theorem, F × t = Δp. Since Δp (change in momentum) is fixed by the ball's speed and mass, increasing the time of contact t proportionally reduces the average force F experienced by the hands. Option C is wrong — the change in momentum is determined by the ball's initial and final velocities, not by how long the hands are drawn back.

questions.stem: A person of mass 60 kg stands on a weighing scale inside a lift that is accelerating downward at 5 m/s². What reading does the scale display? (g = 10 m/s²)

options.option_text: 600 N, equal to the person's true weight at rest on the ground
300 N, the reduced apparent weight under downward acceleration
900 N, the increased apparent weight under downward acceleration
120 N, calculated as mass multiplied only by the lift's acceleration

questions.explanation: B is correct: apparent weight = m(g − a) = 60 × (10 − 5) = 300 N. When the lift accelerates downward, the normal force (scale reading) is less than true weight. Option C is the trap — apparent weight increases only when the lift accelerates upward, using m(g + a).

questions.stem: Blocks of mass 3 kg and 5 kg are connected by a light inextensible string on a smooth horizontal surface. A horizontal force of 16 N is applied to the 5 kg block along the string direction. What is the tension in the string between the two blocks?

options.option_text: 4 N, one-quarter of the applied force on the total system mass
6 N, proportional to the 3 kg block's share of the total system mass
8 N, exactly half of the applied force shared between the blocks
10 N, proportional to the 5 kg block's share of the total system mass

questions.explanation: B is correct: system acceleration a = F/(m₁+m₂) = 16/8 = 2 m/s². Tension acts only on the 3 kg block, so T = 3 × 2 = 6 N. Option C (8 N) is wrong — the string tension is not split equally; it depends on the mass being pulled, not the applied force divided by two.

questions.stem: A simple pendulum hangs from the roof of a train that accelerates uniformly along a horizontal track. If the train's acceleration is 'a' and gravitational acceleration is 'g', the angle θ made by the pendulum string with the vertical satisfies which relation?

options.option_text: tan θ = g/a, ratio of gravitational to horizontal acceleration
tan θ = a/g, ratio of horizontal to gravitational acceleration
tan θ = √(a² + g²)/g, net magnitude scaled by gravitational component
tan θ = a²/g², square of the ratio of both accelerations

questions.explanation: B is correct: in the non-inertial frame of the train, a pseudo-force ma acts backward on the bob. Equilibrium gives T sin θ = ma (horizontal) and T cos θ = mg (vertical), so dividing: tan θ = a/g. Option A inverts the ratio — g/a would mean a faster train tilts the pendulum less, which is physically backward.

questions.stem: A student argues: 'Newton's Third Law says action and reaction are always equal and opposite, so they must always cancel — meaning no net force can ever exist and nothing can accelerate.' Which statement correctly identifies the flaw in this reasoning?

options.option_text: Action-reaction forces are unequal whenever the system has net acceleration
Action-reaction pairs act on different bodies, so they cannot cancel within one body
Newton's Third Law applies only to contact forces, not to field-based forces
The reaction force acts after a brief time delay, preventing instantaneous cancellation

questions.explanation: B is correct: Newton's Third Law pairs always act on two different objects. Net force on a body is determined by all forces acting on that body alone — the reaction acts on the other body. So forces from two different pairs can never cancel each other on the same object. Option D is a common misconception; Newton's Third Law is simultaneous with no time delay — simultaneous action and reaction is actually what makes the law non-trivial.
